description: Passionate software engineers united by our love for space. We combine architecture, development, data, and machine learning to turn complex problems into practical solutions — building software that reaches for the stars and gives back to the planet.
summary: SURCO is a decision-support web app that tells small and mid-size farmers in Colombia which crop cycle, and which 2-3 season rotation, is likely to perform best on their own field under the climate that is coming. The farmer registers and draws the plot on a map. SURCO then combines more than 40 years of NASA POWER climate history with the ECMWF SEAS5 seasonal forecast, the ENSO state, SoilGrids soil data and a crop catalog to score 23 seasonal crops for that exact location and sowing date: expected relative yield, probability of success, irrigation need and heat or cold stress. The best crops are chained into rotations that never repeat a botanical family in consecutive seasons, reward nitrogen-fixing legumes and estimate the water saved compared with monoculture. Everything is explained in plain Spanish ("it does well 8 out of 10 years") with the source of each value, next to official IDEAM rain and drought alerts for the farm. It matters because farmers who plant the same crop every year exhaust their soil and stay exposed to a single bad season, while the satellite and forecast data that could guide them rarely reach the farm in a form they can use.
details:
WHAT IT DOES
SURCO guides a farmer from "where is my plot" to "what should I plant, and in what order". After creating an account and choosing a department and municipality (all 1,122 municipalities of Colombia are loaded), the farmer draws the plot on a map and says whether it has irrigation. The app then shows the current weather and forecast for the farm, ranks the crops that fit the plot for the coming season, proposes the three best rotations of 2-3 seasons, and lists official IDEAM alerts and a drought indicator for the area. The farmer picks a rotation and it is saved as the plan for that plot.

HOW IT WORKS
For the plot's coordinates, a seasonal planner service gathers 365 days of NASA POWER weather before sowing, the NASA POWER climatology since 1981, the ECMWF SEAS5 seasonal forecast (bias-corrected against POWER), the ENSO state (Oceanic Nino Index), SoilGrids soil properties and elevation. An agronomic engine based on FAO-56 (water balance and reference evapotranspiration) and FAO-33 (yield response to water), plus the temperature ranges of each crop phase from our catalog, is run over every member of the forecast ensemble. For each of 23 seasonal crops it returns relative yield (p10/p50/p90), probability of success, irrigation needed in mm and the share of the cycle under heat or cold stress. Crops that do not tolerate the plot's altitude or soil pH are filtered out and shown with the reason.

Rotations are built on top of that ranking. Season 1 uses the forecast; seasons 2 and 3 fall beyond the forecast horizon, so they use how often each crop succeeded in past years on that same plot. Rules: only suitable crops, never the same botanical family twice in a row, and a bonus when a nitrogen-fixing legume comes before another crop. Each rotation gets a grade (A+ to D), a plain-language frequency ("it does well N out of 10 years"), the water saved versus planting the best commercial crop over and over, and the nitrogen the legume leaves in the soil.

We also trained a neural network (PyTorch on an RTX 5060 Ti, exported to ONNX) on the same inputs. It ranked crops slightly better than the baselines but its probabilities were less well calibrated than the agronomic engine, so we documented the comparison and serve the explainable engine. We preferred a number the farmer can trust over a model we could not justify.

BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT
Farmers who repeat one crop every year deplete their soil, concentrate pests and depend on a single season. SURCO turns NASA data and seasonal forecasts, which normally require a data scientist, into one clear answer per plot: what to plant, when, what comes next, how much water it saves and what it gives back to the soil. We start validating in Huila, where rice and coffee are very sensitive to the warm and cold phases of ENSO, but the app works for any municipality in Colombia.

TOOLS
Frontend: Next.js 15, React 19, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS and Leaflet maps. Backend: Java 21 and Spring Boot 4 as a modular monolith with hexagonal architecture, JWT authentication, PostgreSQL with Flyway, and architecture rules enforced by ArchUnit tests. Data and model: Python, PyTorch, ONNX Runtime and a small HTTP microservice. Everything starts with a single Docker Compose command, and GitHub Actions runs the tests on every pull request. The interface was designed in Figma.

CREATIVITY
The farmer is never asked to rank priorities or read charts: the goal is fixed (the best productive result under the expected climate) and every recommendation is phrased the way farmers already talk about risk. Each season says whether it comes from the forecast or from the plot's history, so the tool is honest about what it knows.

WHAT WE CONSIDERED AND CURRENT LIMITS
NASA POWER is a grid of roughly 50 km, not a measurement of the plot, so we combine it with soil and elevation data for the exact point. The results are not yet calibrated against real harvests and the crop catalog has not been validated by an agronomist, so SURCO supports the farmer's decision and does not replace local technical advice. A detailed soil-health view, a what-if climate simulator and satellite soil moisture and vegetation data (SMAP, MODIS) are the next steps.
